package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via phishing, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple variants (not versioned as a software package)
package_info.why_malicious: QBot is a banking trojan and malware loader distributed via phishing campaigns. It is designed to gain initial access to Windows systems, download and execute additional payloads (such as Cobalt Strike and ransomware), steal confidential information, and enable lateral movement within corporate networks.

execution_context.file_location: malicious PDF attachment in phishing email

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PDF attachment masquerading as Office 365/Azure notification with embedded link to download password-protected archive.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user opening the PDF, the document presents a link or button that, when clicked, downloads a password-protected archive from a remote server, enabling delivery of the next stage payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: PDFs in business emails that prompt users to download password-protected archives are a common malware delivery vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate business PDFs rarely require users to download password-protected archives from external sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some secure document workflows use password-protected archives, but typically with prior arrangement and secure channels.

execution_context.trigger: user interaction (extracting and running .wsf file from archive)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Heavily obfuscated JScript code in .wsf file that executes a PowerShell script.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user runs the .wsf file, the obfuscated JScript executes a PowerShell script that attempts to download a DLL from a list of URLs, enabling the next stage of malware delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscated scripts in .wsf files are a common method for evading detection and delivering malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate .wsf files are rare in business workflows and should not download and execute code from the internet.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may use scripts for automation, but not in this context or with obfuscation.

execution_context.file_location: PowerShell command executed by JScript in .wsf file

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PowerShell script that iterates through a list of URLs to download a DLL and execute it.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell script attempts to download a DLL from multiple URLs and then loads and executes the DLL, enabling the QBot payload to run on the victim's system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: PowerShell scripts that download and execute DLLs from the internet are a hallmark of malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell usage should not involve downloading and executing unsigned DLLs from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software deployment tools may use PowerShell for legitimate downloads, but with trusted sources and signatures.
key_indicators: PowerShell downloading DLLs from multiple URLs

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: QBot DLL checks for internet connectivity by executing the PING command, then injects itself into wermgr.exe.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon being loaded, the QBot DLL checks for internet connectivity by running the PING command, then injects itself into the legitimate Windows process wermgr.exe to evade detection and maintain persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLLs that check for internet connectivity and inject themselves into system processes are typical of advanced malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not perform process injection or use system utilities for connectivity checks in this manner.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may check for connectivity, but not inject into unrelated system processes.
key_indicators: Use of PING command for connectivity check

attack_chain.action: Phishing email delivers malicious PDF attachment to victim.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim opens PDF and is prompted to download password-protected archive.

attack_chain.action: Victim downloads and extracts archive, then executes obfuscated .wsf script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Obfuscated JScript runs PowerShell to download DLL.

attack_chain.action: PowerShell script downloads QBot DLL from list of URLs and executes it.
attack_chain.leads_to: QBot DLL is loaded and executed on victim's system.

attack_chain.action: QBot DLL checks for internet connectivity and injects into wermgr.exe for persistence and stealth.
attack_chain.leads_to: QBot operates in background, enabling further payloads and lateral movement.

behavioral_signatures: PDF attachments in emails prompting download of password-protected archives
Execution of .wsf files containing obfuscated JScript
PowerShell scripts downloading and executing DLLs from external URLs
DLLs injecting into legitimate Windows processes (e.g., wermgr.exe)
Use of system commands (PING) for connectivity checks by DLLs
file_indicators: Password-protected ZIP/RAR archives delivered via email
Unexpected DLLs downloaded to user directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections to suspicious or newly registered domains for DLL download
Multiple download attempts from a list of URLs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for emails with PDF attachments that prompt users to download password-protected archives. Flag execution of .wsf files, especially those containing obfuscated code. Detect PowerShell processes that download and execute DLLs from the internet. Watch for DLLs injecting into system processes like wermgr.exe and for use of system commands (e.g., PING) by DLLs. Correlate these behaviors to identify the QBot infection chain.
